subject: biology-hl
topicLabel: C1.3 — Photosynthesis & C4.2 — Transfer of energy (Apr–May unit)

items.stem: The overall equation for photosynthesis is:
items.note: Photosynthesis is respiration reversed — carbon dioxide and water, using light energy captured by chlorophyll, produce glucose and oxygen.

items.stem: During photosynthesis, light energy is converted into:
items.note: The syllabus definition: photosynthesis is the production of carbon compounds from water and carbon dioxide using light energy — light → chemical energy.

items.stem: Oxygen released during photosynthesis comes from:
items.note: Photolysis: water is split at photosystem II to provide electrons, releasing O₂ as a by-product. Confirmed by isotope experiments with ¹⁸O-labelled water.

items.stem: Chlorophyll absorbs light most strongly in which parts of the spectrum?
items.note: Red and blue absorbed; green reflected — which is why leaves look green. The action spectrum (rate) closely matches the absorption spectrum.

items.stem: In the light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle), carbon dioxide combines with:
items.note: Carbon fixation: CO₂ + RuBP → glycerate 3-phosphate (GP), reduced to triose phosphate using ATP and NADPH from the light-dependent reactions.

items.stem: The light-independent reactions take place in the:
items.note: Light-dependent: thylakoid membranes (photosystems). Light-independent: stroma — where the Calvin cycle enzymes are.

items.stem: Which molecule from the light-dependent reactions is needed to reduce GP to triose phosphate?
items.note: The light reactions produce ATP (energy) and NADPH (hydrogen/electrons) — both are used in the Calvin cycle to reduce GP to triose phosphate.

items.stem: Increasing light intensity increases the rate of photosynthesis until:
choices: The leaf is saturated with glucose
Another factor becomes limiting (e.g. CO₂ concentration or temperature)
items.note: The graph plateaus at the limiting factor switch. Beyond the plateau, excess light can even reduce the rate (photoinhibition).

items.stem: Chromatography of leaf pigments separates them because each pigment has a different:
items.note: Pigments dissolve differently and travel different distances up the paper — Rf = distance travelled by pigment / distance by solvent.

items.stem: The energy losses between trophic levels in a food chain are mainly due to:
choices: Heat from respiration, uneaten parts and excretion
items.note: Only ~10% of energy passes to the next level: organisms lose most energy through cellular respiration (heat), plus uneaten/indigestible material and excretion.

items.stem: Food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels because:
choices: Not enough energy remains after the losses at each level
Consumers need less energy than producers
items.note: Energy transfer is ~10% per level — after 4–5 levels too little energy remains to sustain another population.

items.stem: Pyramids of energy are always upright (widest at the base) because:
choices: Producers are always larger than consumers
Energy always decreases when transferred between trophic levels
Energy can be recycled between levels
items.note: Unlike pyramids of numbers (which can invert), energy always decreases — the second law of thermodynamics guarantees it.

items.stem: Which organisms convert organic matter in dead organisms back into CO₂ and inorganic nutrients?
items.note: Saprotrophs secrete enzymes and absorb externally digested products; detritivores ingest dead matter internally. Both recycle nutrients in the carbon cycle.

items.stem: In the carbon cycle, photosynthesis and respiration respectively:
items.note: Photosynthesis fixes atmospheric CO₂ into carbon compounds; respiration releases it back. Burning fossil fuels adds — the imbalance driving climate change.

items.stem: Outline the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis, including where they occur and their products.
markscheme: Occur in the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast (1)
Chlorophyll in photosystem II absorbs light → electrons excited (1)
Photolysis of water provides replacement electrons, releasing O₂ (1)
Electrons pass along the electron transport chain → proton gradient → ATP by chemiosmosis/photophosphorylation (1)
Products: ATP and NADPH passed to the Calvin cycle (1)
items.tactic: Location → process in order (absorption, photolysis, electron transport, products) — the products (ATP + NADPH) link forward to the Calvin cycle, so mention them.

items.stem: Explain why only about 10% of the energy in one trophic level is available to the next, and state one consequence for the structure of food chains.
markscheme: Energy is lost as heat from cellular respiration (1)
Not all food is eaten / not all parts are digestible → egestion (1)
Consequence: only ~10% passed on, so food chains are limited to 4–5 trophic levels (1)
Pyramids of energy are always upright (1)
items.tactic: Three loss mechanisms (respiration, egestion, excretion/uneaten) + one consequence. 'Heat from respiration' is the big one — always include it.
